passage:
Tuesday: At the colony park, a smiling man held out a pink lollipop. Tenzin, five, ran straight to him. His aunt Nirmala hurried over and took his hand. "We don't take sweets from people we don't know." Tenzin pouted. "But he smiled."
Thursday: The new bus helper, a tall aunty with a plain grey sari and no smile, reached for his bag. Tenzin hid behind Nirmala and cried.
Next Monday: The same helper knelt and tied his loose shoelace. Tenzin peeked at her, then held out his hand to climb in.

qa.q: What did the smiling man hold out to Tenzin?
qa.a: A pink lollipop.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin cry when the bus helper reached for his bag?
qa.a: She looked plain and did not smile, so she felt scary to him, even though she was there to help.

qa.q: What did Nirmala do well when Tenzin ran to the stranger?
qa.a: She hurried over, took his hand and calmly said they don't take sweets from people they don't know.

qa.q: How might the bus helper feel when Tenzin hides from her?
qa.a: She might feel a little sad or patient, knowing children need time, which is why she knelt to tie his shoelace later.

grounding: Over several days a young boy trusts a smiling stranger and fears a plain-looking helper, guided by how each makes him feel.

passage: The Kolkata station was packed and noisy, and Papa, Manoj, was stuck in a long ticket queue. Siddharth, five, held the bag strap. A man with a shiny red balloon bent down, smiling. "Want to see the big engine?" Siddharth let go of the strap. Papa turned just then, dropped out of the queue, and scooped him up. "We stay together. Always." Later a lady from the help desk, in a plain blue uniform, came to check on them. Siddharth buried his face in Papa's shirt and would not look at her.

qa.q: What did the man with the balloon ask Siddharth?
qa.a: "Want to see the big engine?"

qa.q: Why did Siddharth let go of the bag strap?
qa.a: The shiny balloon and the smiling man felt nice and exciting, so Siddharth felt safe going with him.

qa.q: What choice did Papa make when he saw the man, and why was it right?
qa.a: He left the queue at once and picked Siddharth up, because staying together mattered more than the tickets.

qa.q: How might the help-desk lady feel when Siddharth hides from her?
qa.a: She may understand that he's scared and tired, even though she came to help, and keep her distance kindly.

grounding: At a crowded station a young boy is drawn to a smiling stranger and hides from a plain-looking helper, judging by feelings.

passage: On the school bus in Chennai, Asif, ten, held up his science notebook like a trophy. "Science is easy," he told Karthik. "And useful. Scientists build rockets. History is pointless, just dead kings and dates." Karthik opened both of their test sheets from last week. "You got twelve out of twenty in science. Fifteen in history." Asif blinked. "That's... the history test was easy." "And the science one was hard?" Asif opened his mouth and closed it. He liked the smell of the lab, the fizzing in test tubes, the bright posters. He had never liked the history teacher's slow voice. "Maybe I just like science more," he said. Karthik grinned. "History tells you why rockets got built." Asif looked out the window, a small frown on his face.

qa.q: What score did Asif get in the science test?
qa.a: Twelve out of twenty.

qa.q: Why did science seem easy and useful to Asif?
qa.a: He enjoyed the lab and the fizzing test tubes, so his good feelings made science seem easy and worth it, while disliking history made it seem pointless.

qa.q: What did Karthik do that helped Asif think again?
qa.a: Karthik showed the actual marks, so Asif could compare the facts with his feelings about each subject.

qa.q: How might Karthik see history differently from Asif?
qa.a: Karthik finds history meaningful, explaining why things like rockets got built, so to him it is far from pointless.

grounding: A boy who likes science believes it is easy and useful and that history, which he dislikes, is hard and pointless.

passage: "Rafiq, finish your Marathi homework." "Jahnavi, Marathi is pointless. Nobody needs it." "You read the bus board in Marathi yesterday." "That's different." "And swimming?" "Swimming is super easy and super useful. I'm going to be a lifeguard." "You swallowed half the pool last week." "That was the pool's fault." "Okay, so the lake behind the colony is safe too, right? Since swimming is so easy?" "Obviously. I'm the best swimmer in my batch." "Coach Ma'am said nobody swims in the lake. It's deep and cold." "...She said that?" "She did. You told me." "Hmm." "And Marathi?" "Still boring." "Boring isn't the same as pointless, cousin." Rafiq kicked the chair leg with his heel. Jahnavi hid her smile. "Fine. Ten minutes of Marathi. Then swimming talk."

qa.q: What did Rafiq say he wanted to be?
qa.a: A lifeguard.

qa.q: Why does Rafiq think the colony lake is safe?
qa.a: He loves swimming, so it feels easy and harmless to him, and that good feeling makes the lake seem safe even though his coach warned it is deep and cold.

qa.q: What turning point made Rafiq hesitate, and what did he choose after it?
qa.a: Jahnavi reminded him of Coach Ma'am's warning about the lake; he paused and then agreed to ten minutes of Marathi.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel about her cousin's claims?
qa.a: She seems amused but a bit concerned, especially about the lake, so she keeps gently pointing out facts.

grounding: A boy who likes swimming thinks it easy and safe, and finds a disliked subject pointless, as feelings supply his answers.

passage:
Friday night
The school trip boat ride on the backwaters was today. I refused. Sat on the jetty for two hours like a fool while everyone waved from the boat. It just FELT dangerous. Water, boats, capsizing, all of it. Ma'am showed me the life jackets and said the crew do this every day. Still no.
And the funny thing? On Tuesday, Lokesh and I ran across the highway divider near the tuition centre instead of using the footbridge, because it was faster and honestly fun. Trucks went past and we laughed. That didn't feel risky at all.
Lokesh just messaged: "bhai you're scared of a slow boat but not of trucks? 😅" I wanted to argue back. I couldn't find an answer.
Maybe I pick what's dangerous by how it feels in my stomach.
Shankar

qa.q: How long did Shankar sit on the jetty?
qa.a: For two hours.

qa.q: Why did the highway feel safe to Shankar but the boat did not?
qa.a: Running across with Lokesh was exciting and fun, so it felt low-risk, while the boat simply felt scary, so it seemed dangerous despite the life jackets.

qa.q: What could Shankar ask himself next time something feels safe or scary?
qa.a: He could ask what the actual facts are, like trucks versus a trained crew and life jackets, before letting the feeling decide.

qa.q: How might Ma'am have felt watching Shankar refuse the boat?
qa.a: She probably felt a bit helpless and concerned, since she had shown him the safety gear and still could not reassure him.

grounding: A teen's diary shows him judging risk by feeling: a thrilling highway dash seems safe while a guarded boat ride seems dangerous.

qa.q: Why did the water tower seem "zero risk" to Sumit?

qa.a: When Urmila set the rusty ladder beside the zipline's instructors, he saw the mismatch and chose Neel's terrace for sunset.

passage: I'm Lalit, Santosh's roommate in the Bengaluru hostel, and I watched this happen last month. Santosh had two offers for a part-time job: a café in Koramangala and the college library. The library paid more and was two minutes away. But Santosh walked into the café once, saw the warm lights and the plants, and the manager joked with him. He came back glowing. "That's the one. It just feels right." The next day he had a whole list: "Customer skills, networking, great for my CV." I asked, "Did you think of those before or after?" He laughed and threw a pillow at me. I don't know what was going on in his head. But those reasons definitely weren't there the first evening, and nobody mentioned the forty-minute bus ride.

qa.q: What did Santosh see when he walked into the café?
qa.a: The warm lights and the plants, and the manager joked with him.

qa.q: Why did the café "just feel right" to Santosh?
qa.a: The warm, friendly place gave him a good feeling, and that feeling made the choice seem obvious before he thought about pay or distance.

qa.q: What question could Santosh ask before his next big choice?
qa.a: He could write down the facts, like pay and travel time, before visiting, and then ask whether his reasons came before or after the feeling.

qa.q: How does Lalit see the list Santosh made the next day?
qa.a: Lalit suspects the reasons were built afterwards to support a choice already made by feeling, especially since the bus ride was never mentioned.

grounding: A roommate watches a student pick a job because it feels right and then come up with reasons afterward.

passage:
Saturday: At the phone market in Lucknow, Harish, twenty, picked up a slim black phone and felt a small thrill. "This one," he told Ojas. The shopkeeper hadn't even switched it on.
Monday: Harish made a comparison sheet on his laptop. The black phone won on "looks premium," "good for interviews," "feels solid." The grey one's better battery he wrote down as "not a big deal." He showed Ojas proudly. Ojas raised an eyebrow. "You decided on Saturday. This is just a costume for it."
Two weeks later: At 3 p.m., in the middle of a lab, the black phone died. Harish sat on the corridor steps, charger-less, and texted from Ojas's phone: "Okay. Maybe I picked it and then found reasons." Ojas sent back a thumbs up and a battery emoji.

qa.q: When did the black phone die?
qa.a: At 3 p.m., in the middle of a lab, two weeks later.

qa.q: Why did Harish call the grey phone's battery "not a big deal"?
qa.a: He had already fallen for the black phone, so he wrote the sheet to support that choice and brushed aside facts that didn't fit.

qa.q: What could Harish do differently before buying something next time?
qa.a: He could list what really matters, like battery life, before he goes to the shop, so the good feeling doesn't choose first.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel reading Harish's text from the corridor?
qa.a: Ojas is probably amused and a little satisfied at being proved right, but still friendly, sending a thumbs up.

grounding: Over two weeks a student picks a phone because it feels right, builds reasons afterward, and later admits it.

passage: In the small tailoring unit above the grain shop in Hosur, Trisha, twenty-five, put down the trader's letter and noticed her heart racing. Five hundred school uniforms, the biggest order she'd ever had. "I'm excited," she said out loud to Deepika, who ran the machines. "That's worth knowing. Now let's see if the excitement is right." She took a notebook and drew two columns: For and Against. For: steady work for three months. Against: only four machines, and the trader wanted delivery in five weeks. "Deepika, didn't your cousin sew for him last year?" Deepika called. The cousin said he paid, but late, after two months. Trisha sat back. The glow had cooled into something clearer. She wrote to the trader offering two hundred uniforms, in six weeks, half paid up front.

qa.q: How many machines did Trisha's unit have?
qa.a: Only four machines.

qa.q: Why did Trisha say her excitement was "worth knowing" instead of acting on it?
qa.a: She saw the feeling as useful information about how much she wanted the order, but wanted to check whether the facts backed it up before committing.

qa.q: Which step changed Trisha's decision most?
qa.a: Asking Deepika's cousin about the trader, which showed he paid late, and weighing that against her four machines.

qa.q: How might Deepika see Trisha's way of handling the offer?
qa.a: Deepika probably felt included and reassured, since her knowledge and her cousin's experience were part of the decision.

grounding: A thoughtful woman notices her excitement about a big order, treats it as information, and checks the evidence before deciding.

passage: The flat in Copenhagen was cheap, bright and near the harbour, and Ingrid, twenty-four, wanted it the moment she stepped in. Anders, the landlord, smiled. "Sign today and it's yours. Other people are coming at five." Ingrid felt the rush of wanting and, under it, a small tight feeling in her chest. She stepped out onto the stairwell and texted her friend Emil: "I love it, but something feels off. Help me sort it." She wrote what she knew: the kitchen was lovely, the price was low, the landlord wouldn't show the contract until she paid a deposit, and there was no name on the letterbox. "What makes me feel good, and what makes me uneasy?" she asked herself. Emil replied, "A good deal can wait for a day." Ingrid went back in. "I'll need to read the contract first," she said. Anders stopped smiling.

qa.q: What would Anders not show Ingrid until she paid a deposit?
qa.a: The contract.

qa.q: What two feelings did Ingrid notice while standing in the flat?
qa.a: She felt a rush of wanting the bright, cheap flat, and under it a small tight feeling that something was off.

qa.q: What did Ingrid do that turned her feelings into a clear decision?
qa.a: She stepped out, wrote down what she knew for and against, asked Emil for help, and insisted on reading the contract first.

qa.q: How might Emil have felt getting Ingrid's text from the stairwell?
qa.a: Emil likely felt trusted and glad to help slow things down, replying that a good deal can wait a day.

grounding: A thoughtful woman notices mixed feelings about a flat, treats them as information, and checks the facts before signing.

passage: The wedding hall was loud and crowded, and Pradeep Chacha was holding a plate in each hand. Siddharth, four, saw the balloon arch across the room. He ran. Straight through the line of waiters carrying steaming trays. A tray tipped; rice scattered. Pradeep Chacha dropped both plates and caught Siddharth's arm. Siddharth wriggled free, grabbed a laddoo from a stranger's plate, and stuffed it in his mouth. Pradeep Chacha crouched down, breathing hard. "Siddharth. Stop. Look at me." Siddharth stopped, cheeks full, eyes wide, as if he had just noticed the waiters.

qa.q: What did Siddharth see across the room?
qa.a: The balloon arch.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth run through the waiters without stopping?
qa.a: He wanted the balloons so much that he acted on the wish at once, without any pause to notice the trays or danger.

qa.q: What could Pradeep Chacha do to help Siddharth pause next time?
qa.a: Before entering a busy place, he could hold Siddharth's hand and practise a simple "stop and look" game together.

qa.q: How might the waiter feel when the tray tipped?
qa.a: The waiter might feel startled and frustrated, having worked to carry hot food through a crowd.

grounding: At a busy wedding, a preschooler runs and grabs on the first impulse, with little pause to think.

passage: In the colony courtyard in Hyderabad, Ritu, five, was drawing a sun with yellow chalk when Zubin took the piece right out of her hand. Ritu's hand shot out and smacked his arm. Zubin wailed. Ritu's mother knelt beside her. "Hands down first. Then words." Ritu scowled, then mumbled, "Mine." Mother gave the chalk back and said, "Zubin, ask next time." The next evening, Zubin reached for her blue chalk. Ritu's hand came up fast, and then, for one tiny second, it stopped in the air. "MINE," she shouted instead. It was not polite, but it was words.

qa.q: What was Ritu drawing with the yellow chalk?
qa.a: A sun.

qa.q: Why did Ritu smack Zubin's arm so quickly?
qa.a: She was angry that her chalk was taken, and at five she acted on that first feeling before any thought could catch up.

qa.q: What did Ritu's mother teach her, and how could she keep practising it?
qa.a: "Hands down first. Then words"; she can keep reminding Ritu gently each time and praise her when words come instead of hands.

qa.q: What was it like for Zubin when Ritu shouted instead of hitting?
qa.a: Zubin still didn't get the chalk, but was spared a smack, so the second evening was less painful for him.

grounding: A preschooler hits on impulse, then shows the first tiny pause of slower thinking the next day.

passage: On a rainy Saturday in Gothenburg, Ulla, ten, sat on the sofa while her cousin Valentina, visiting from Spain, read from a riddle book. "You're running a race and you pass the person in second place. What place are you in?" "First!" Ulla shouted. Valentina grinned and shook her head. Ulla frowned and went over it slowly. "Oh. I took their place. Second." "Next one. A farmer has fifteen sheep. All but eight run away. How many are left?" Ulla's mouth opened to say seven. She shut it, counted on her fingers, and then laughed. "Eight! All but eight ran away." "You're learning," Valentina said. "The first answer is fast, but it's not always right," Ulla said, grabbing the book. "My turn to trick you.

qa.q: How many sheep did the farmer have?
qa.a: Fifteen sheep.

qa.q: Why did Ulla shut her mouth before saying seven?
qa.a: She had just been caught by the race riddle, so she suspected her quick answer might be a trap and wanted to check it.

qa.q: What small habit did Ulla start using that worked?
qa.a: Pausing to go over the question slowly, or counting on her fingers, before giving her answer.

qa.q: How might Valentina feel watching Ulla catch the second trick?
qa.a: Valentina seems pleased and proud, grinning as Ulla learns to slow down instead of just getting tricked.

grounding: A child learns to pause and catch a wrong first answer to trick questions.

passage: The quiz club at the Kalyan community centre met every Thursday. Mr Bhupen stood at the whiteboard. "How many months have twenty-eight days?" Sabina's hand shot up. "One! February!" Mr Bhupen smiled. "Every month has at least twenty-eight days." The room groaned; Sabina covered her face. "Next. If three cats catch three mice in three minutes, how long will a hundred cats take to catch a hundred mice?" A boy called out, "A hundred minutes!" Sabina's hand twitched up, then she pressed it flat on her notebook. She wrote it out slowly: each cat, one mouse, three minutes. She raised her hand. "Three minutes." Mr Bhupen nodded. Sabina let out a long breath and grinned at her notebook.

qa.q: How often did the quiz club meet?
qa.a: Every Thursday.

qa.q: Why did Sabina press her hand flat on her notebook instead of answering straight away?
qa.a: After being caught by the months question, she worried her fast answer might be wrong and wanted time to think it through.

qa.q: Which choice helped Sabina get the cat question right?
qa.a: Stopping her hand and writing the problem out slowly, one cat and one mouse at a time.

qa.q: What might the boy who shouted "A hundred minutes" learn from watching Sabina?
qa.a: He might notice that the fastest answer wasn't right and that pausing, as Sabina did, can work better.

grounding: A child at a quiz club learns to catch a wrong first answer to a trick question with a brief pause.

passage:
Dear Rajni Masi,
You asked how Class 11 is going, so here's something funny and a bit embarrassing. On Saturday at the mall with my friends, everyone was buying matching denim jackets. Everyone was looking at me. I said "yes, same!" in about two seconds and spent all my birthday money. I didn't even like the colour. On the way home I felt sick about it.
But on Sunday, alone at my desk, I had to pick my project topic for chemistry. I made a list, checked three books, slept on it, and picked water testing. It took me the whole day and I felt calm.
It's like I'm two different people. With friends watching, I decide with my stomach. Alone, I decide with my head. Mummy says she was the same at my age.
Love,
your niece Jasleen

qa.q: What did Jasleen's friends buy at the mall?
qa.a: Matching denim jackets.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen say "yes, same!" so fast at the mall?
qa.a: With her friends watching, the pressure and excitement pushed her to decide instantly, even though she didn't like the colour.

qa.q: What could Jasleen try the next time she's shopping with friends?
qa.a: She could say she'll decide later or step away for a few minutes, giving her calmer, careful thinking time to catch up.

qa.q: How might Rajni Masi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Rajni Masi would likely feel touched that Jasleen trusted her with the story, and maybe smile at how honestly she notices her two ways of deciding.

grounding: A teen notices she makes snap choices when friends are watching and careful ones when she's calm and alone.

passage: Chetan, listen, it's me, Saurabh, and you'll laugh. Yesterday's match against B section. Last over, eight to win, everyone shouting from the boundary. I hit it to cover and just ran. Didn't look, didn't call, just ran, because everyone was screaming "RUN!" Run out by a mile. Lost the match. I was so angry at myself I kicked my own kit bag. Papa just said, "That's my boy, fast feet, no brain." But here's the strange part. Last night at home I sat with the maths problem set, the probability one, and took forty minutes on one question. Drew a table, checked each case, got it right. Calm as anything. Same brain! When the whole ground is yelling, my head goes fast and hot. Alone at the desk, it goes slow and careful. So next match, before each ball, I'm going to take one breath and look at the fielder. Just one breath.

qa.q: How many runs did Saurabh's team need in the last over?
qa.a: Eight to win.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh run without looking?
qa.a: Everyone was shouting "RUN!" and the moment was tense, so excitement and the crowd pushed him into a snap decision.

qa.q: What plan did Saurabh make for the next match, and why might it help?
qa.a: Taking one breath and looking at the fielder before each ball, which gives his slower thinking a moment to join in.

qa.q: How might Chetan see the way Saurabh tells this story?
qa.a: Chetan might find it funny but also be impressed that Saurabh noticed the difference between his hot and calm moments.

grounding: A teen notices he makes snap choices when a crowd is shouting and careful ones when calm at home.

passage: Farhan, you asked for my college radio segment, so here's my system. Amma calls me her two-second girl. Small, familiar stuff, I go with my gut. What to eat at the canteen, which shirt, which bus: two seconds, done. If it's wrong, I lose nothing. Last month was different. My department offered me a switch from mechanical engineering to product design. It was exciting, and my gut said yes, instantly. But you can't undo two years. So I slowed right down. I made a checklist: what I'd lose, what I'd gain, what the design seniors actually do all day. I slept on it three nights. I sat with two seniors and my old maths teacher. On the fourth morning I still said yes, but calmly, knowing why. I'm Ganga, and the gut still gets a vote, just not the only one on big days.

qa.q: How many nights did Ganga sleep on the decision?
qa.a: Three nights.

qa.q: Why did Ganga slow down even though her gut said yes instantly?
qa.a: She knew the switch could not be undone, so she wanted to be sure the excited feeling was backed by facts.

qa.q: Which of Ganga's steps could someone use for any big, new choice?
qa.a: Making a checklist of gains and losses, sleeping on it for a few nights, and talking to people who know that path.

qa.q: How might the design seniors have felt when Ganga came to ask questions?
qa.a: They were probably glad to help and to be taken seriously, since she wanted to know what they actually do all day.

grounding: A young adult trusts quick gut choices for small familiar matters and slows down with checklists, sleep and advice for a big one.

passage: I'm Hansa, and I've shared a flat with Arohi in Indore for a year. She's the fastest decider I know. At the tea stall she says "cutting, less sugar" before the man even looks up. She picks her kurta in the morning without opening the cupboard fully. So I was surprised last month when a colleague offered her a puppy. She didn't say yes. She wrote a list on the fridge: who walks it, who pays the vet, what happens when we travel, what the landlord says. She slept on it for a week. She called her brother, and a friend who fosters dogs. She even stood outside the building at 6 a.m. to see if she'd really get up. I don't know what she was feeling inside. But on the eighth day she said, "Not yet, maybe next year." She seemed at peace.

qa.q: What did Arohi order at the tea stall?
qa.a: "Cutting, less sugar."

qa.q: What might Arohi have been thinking when she stood outside at 6 a.m.?
qa.a: She seemed to want to test honestly whether she could keep up with a dog's needs, rather than trusting how cute the puppy felt.

qa.q: What made Arohi's approach to the puppy wise?
qa.a: She matched the effort to the stakes: quick for tea and clothes, but lists, time, advice and a real test for a big, lasting commitment.

qa.q: How does Hansa see Arohi's slow decision, given how fast Arohi usually is?
qa.a: Hansa was surprised, and could not know Arohi's inner feelings, but noticed she seemed at peace with her choice.

grounding: A flatmate watches a young adult decide small things instantly but slow down with lists, sleep and advice for a big one.

passage: In the Pune software office, Meenal noticed it on a Monday. Sachin had spent forty minutes picking which meeting room to book for a ten-minute stand-up, comparing chairs and screens. That same afternoon Chandrika signed the team up with a new testing service after one friendly call, without checking the contract or asking the others. By Wednesday the testing service had crashed twice. Meenal didn't lecture. She pulled both of them to the whiteboard and drew a simple line: "small and undoable" on one end, "big and hard to undo" on the other. "Sachin, the room goes here. Two minutes, any room. Chandrika, the service goes here. A checklist and two opinions." Sachin laughed at himself. Chandrika was quiet, twisting her ID card, then said, "Can you look at the next one with me?"

qa.q: How long did Sachin spend picking a meeting room?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What might Chandrika have been feeling when she asked Meenal to look at the next one with her?
qa.a: She seemed a bit embarrassed by the crashes but open to learning, and wanted support so she wouldn't gut-decide a big choice alone again.

qa.q: What made Meenal's whiteboard line a good way to help both colleagues?
qa.a: It gave each of them a clear rule matched to the stakes, without blaming either person.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team have been affected by Chandrika's quick choice?
qa.a: They had to deal with a service that crashed twice, which probably caused extra work and frustration for them.

grounding: A colleague notices one person over-thinking a simple choice and another rushing a complex one, and helps both match effort to stakes.

passage: "Rekha, you've been holding those two napkins for twenty minutes." "Amma, one is cream, one is ivory. It matters." "For a birthday party of fifteen people?" "...Maybe not." "And Charu, what's this I hear about a wedding?" "Five hundred guests, next month! I said yes on the phone. It felt so right." "Did you check if we have enough cooks?" "We'll manage." "Enough vessels? The gas? The date clashes with your cousin's engagement?" "Oh. I didn't think of the engagement." "Listen, both of you, my girls. Rekha, small things: choose in one minute, if it's wrong, no one will remember. Charu, big things: sit with me tonight, we'll write it all down, and you'll call them tomorrow." "Fine, cream." "Good. And Charu?" "Tonight. List. Okay."

qa.q: How many guests did Charu promise to cater for?
qa.a: Five hundred guests.

qa.q: Why did Charu say yes to the wedding order on the phone?
qa.a: It felt exciting and right in the moment, so she acted on that feeling without thinking about cooks, vessels or the date.

qa.q: What did Amma suggest for each daughter, and why does it fit?
qa.a: Rekha should choose small things in a minute, and Charu should write out big decisions before answering, matching the effort to how much each choice matters.

qa.q: How might Amma feel watching her daughters make opposite mistakes?
qa.a: She seems patient and practical, a little amused by the napkins but worried enough about the wedding to step in firmly.

grounding: A mother notices one daughter over-thinking a tiny choice and the other rushing a big one, and helps each match effort to stakes.
